items.title: A proton in an aromatic ring 'feels' a different magnetic field
items.claim: Switch on a strong magnetic field around a benzene ring and the circulating pi electrons generate their own magnetic field. Protons ATTACHED to the ring sit in a region where this ring current adds to the external field. Protons ABOVE the ring sit in a region where it subtracts.
items.prompt: What does this predict about NMR chemical shifts?

options.text: All aromatic protons appear at the same shift

Aromatic ring protons resonate at unusually high chemical shifts (~7 ppm); a proton positioned ABOVE the ring (as in 18-annulene's inner H's) appears at NEGATIVE shift — a diagnostic test for aromaticity
Aromatic protons don't appear in NMR spectra
Chemical shifts have nothing to do with the molecule's geometry

items.reveal_title: The ring current — aromaticity made visible
items.reveal:
In an aromatic ring, delocalised pi electrons circulate around the ring when placed in an external magnetic field. By Lenz's law this induces an opposing magnetic field that loops through the centre of the ring and outwards above and below.

Protons in the ring's plane (attached to the ring) sit where the induced field reinforces the external field — they are 'deshielded' and resonate at high chemical shift (~6 to 8 ppm).

In larger aromatic molecules like 18-annulene, the inner protons sit above the ring plane and experience the opposing component — their NMR signals appear at NEGATIVE chemical shift (around minus 3 ppm). This is the most direct physical evidence aromaticity exists.
items.why: Chemical shift is taught as a lookup table. It's really a probe of the molecule's three-dimensional electronic structure.

items.title: Benzene has no double bonds — and no single bonds
items.claim: Draw benzene the textbook way and you get alternating single and double bonds. But every carbon-carbon bond in benzene is exactly the same length: 139 picometres.
items.prompt: If a normal C-C single bond is 154 pm and a C=C double bond is 134 pm, what is going on?

options.text: The bonds flip back and forth so fast we measure the average
The six pi electrons are delocalised into a ring above and below the plane of the carbons — every bond has bond order 1.5
Benzene actually has three single and three double bonds; the textbook value of 139 pm is wrong
Each carbon has one and a half hydrogens on average

items.reveal_title: Aromaticity — delocalisation as a real, measurable thing
items.reveal:
Each carbon in benzene is sp2 hybridised. It contributes one electron to a p-orbital perpendicular to the ring. These six p-orbitals overlap sideways all the way around, forming two continuous doughnut-shaped pi clouds — one above the ring, one below.

The Kekulé structure with alternating bonds is not 'wrong' — it is one of two resonance structures. But the molecule is the average, with all bonds equivalent. Aromaticity also explains why benzene resists addition reactions that would break the ring's stability.
items.why: The line-and-double-line notation is a 19th century compromise. Quantum mechanics shows the real picture: delocalised electrons in a ring.
